---
title: "Matrix Phylogeny"
description: "An original worked mathematical lesson corresponding to MML §4.7."
---

**Reference:** *Mathematics for Machine Learning*, Chapter 4, §4.7. The teaching example and explanation here are original.

## Why we need this concept

Different matrix classes form a hierarchy: being square, symmetric, positive definite or orthogonal determines which decomposition or inverse is available. The book uses 'phylogeny' as a taxonomy of these relationships.

## Derive the structure

$$
\mathrm{SPD}_n\subset\mathrm{Sym}_n\subset\mathbb R^{n\times n},\qquad A\in\mathrm{SPD}_n\Longrightarrow A=LL^\top
$$

Check the shapes and conditions in this statement before applying it. The formula encodes the exact relationship to reason about, rather than replacing a derivation with a library call.

## Worked example

A=diag(2,3) is symmetric, positive definite, invertible and diagonalizable. B=[[1,2],[0,1]] is square and invertible but nonsymmetric and not diagonalizable over R: these branches are not equivalent.

## Interpretation and limitations

The inclusion graph is a taxonomy, not a biological evolution process. An arbitrary rectangular real matrix has an SVD but no ordinary square-matrix determinant. Some properties overlap without forming one simple chain.

## Challenge

Is every orthogonal matrix symmetric? Try a 90-degree rotation matrix as a counterexample.
